title: Hosting flexibility matrix + retrospective — mid-market e‑com POC
summary: Workshop takeaways and a compact decision matrix for a mid-market e-commerce POC that needs low p99 latency during peak events, EU data residency for checkout flows, and predictable cost for growth. This doc captures the matrix of options we evaluated (hosted / dedicated / private), the hybrid recommendation, quantitative knobs, and an experimental rollout plan.
decision_log:
2025-02-12: Kickoff workshop — gathered constraints from customer (peak events, EU checkout, SLOs).
2025-02-14: Shortlist three deployment patterns and mapped to cost/latency/risk.
2025-02-20: Chose hybrid primary-hosted + reserved-dedicated-burst + private-EU for PII as canonical proposal (pending infra sizing).
2025-02-25: Follow-up benchmark run (50 concurrent sessions simulating Black Friday traffic) showed hosted baseline p99=170ms, dedicated-only baseline p99=120ms. Decision: use hosted for steady-state, dedicated for burst window.
2025-02-28: Customer asked for explicit fallback behavior for region outages; added routing policy: EU checkout -> private (when available) -> dedicated -> hosted (in that order).
architecture_options:
We evaluated three main architecture patterns and several intermediate hybrids.

Option A — Hosted-first (SaaS API):
- Pros: fastest onboarding, zero infra ops for customer, seamless autoscaling.
- Cons: p99 under high bursts can breach 150ms target, limited control over data residency without private endpoints.
- Typical config: Redwood hosted model v1.2, streaming enabled, autoscaling policy aggressive, prefix cache TTL=5s.

Option B — Dedicated-reserved pool (customer-owned throughput):
- Pros: predictable throughput and p99, capacity guarantees via reserved GPUs, better cost at sustained high QPS.
- Cons: commit fees, ops for capacity planning, slower scale to unexpected bursts unless burst pools available.
- Typical config: 4x A100-80GB equivalents reserved, autoscale burst pool + queued fallback to hosted, KV-cache warmup during canary.

Option C — Private (VPC/on-prem) for regulated flows:
- Pros: full data residency, KMS/HSM integration, on-prem auditability.
- Cons: long lead time, infra ops for customer, lower flexibility for fast scale.
- Typical config: private control plane, H100 nodes for inference of the larger model, strict egress rules.

Recommended hybrid (for this customer):
- Primary: Hosted for general browsing and personalization (steady-state).
- Reserved Dedicated: Keep a dedicated reserved pool sized for expected Black Friday baseline (50% of expected peak).
- Burst via Hosted: Allow hosted to absorb overflow with rate-limited tokens and circuit-breaker policies.
- Private EU slice: Deploy a private instance handling checkout and any PII-sensitive prompts; route via token-level policy so only checkout flows hit private endpoints.
- Routing policy: route_by_route + region_prefer + fallback_priority configured in the control plane.
quantitative_estimates:
Baseline assumptions: average request = 120 tokens generated, 3 requests/session, 10k daily sessions steady, peak 120k sessions during promo window.
Estimated token volume (steady): ~3.6M tokens/day. Peak day: ~43.2M tokens.
Cost heuristics (ballpark): hosted-only: $1,200/day during peak events (due to autoscaled GPUs and egress), dedicated-reserved (4x A100 eq): ~$45k/mo reserved + ~$800/day for maintenance/ops, private EU (small cluster): ~$25k/mo infra + setup.
Latency targets & measured: target p99 ≤ 150ms for browsing flows, target p99 ≤ 100ms for checkout flows. Benchmark results: hosted p99=170ms (peak sim), dedicated p99=120ms, private-EU p99=95ms (checkout profile).
SLA tradeoff: to guarantee 150ms p99 during peak, need dedicated baseline = ~60% of peak QPS + hosted burst cap at 40% with preferential routing.
evaluation_plan:
1) Infra spike test: provision 2x dedicated reservation (pilot) and replay production trace for 2h at 70% expected peak. Measure p50/p95/p99, cost delta, and contention.
2) End-to-end canary: route 5% of production traffic to dedicated pool for 48h during a low-risk window. Monitor model output quality, perf and error rates.
3) Privacy path test: deploy private-EU minimum viable cluster and run checkout flow for 1 week with synthetic PII to validate KMS/HSM integration.
4) Failure injection: simulate EU region outage and verify fallback sequence (private->dedicated->hosted) and customer-visible latency degradation.
5) Post-experiment retrospective to tune cache TTL, batch window, and replica count.
Primary metrics: p99 latency, cost per 1M tokens, tail error rate (5xx), model hallucination rate on checkout prompts (as measured by eval prompts).

discussion_notes:
Workshop fragments / verbatim: 'We cannot have checkout latency slip more than 20ms' — customer PM.
Customer infra: uses GCP europe-west4 primarily, internal SSO and KMS.
Key unresolved: exact sizing for burst capacity and whether customer will accept minute-level cold starts for private cluster scaling.
Notes to self: confirm whether quantized 4-bit model variant affects checkout quality (sample eval set needed).
Slack threads referenced: #solutions-ecom-poc, #infra-pilot-requests.
Risks called out during workshop: data residency compliance timelines, on-call burn if dedicated reserved underutilized, and rate-limiter misconfig causing 429 cascades.
retrospective_notes:
What went well: clear routing matrix simplified the conversation; customer liked hybrid because it balances cost and residency.
What we should change: run earlier small-scale private-EU test (we delayed and it added time), capture more workload shape percentiles (p99.9) for better reserve sizing.
Quick wins: reduce cache TTL for personalization to lower token counts during browses; enable prefix/KV caching on dedicated warmup.
Longer items: productize a 'checkout slice' template to speed future similar deals (predefined route_by_route + KMS integration template).
